Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
I work hard at keeping busy with other things

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

vignette: Karim remembered the night the Chicago textile warehouse caught fire during a supplier’s rooftop showcase. He had been arranging silk bolts when the blast severed the main gas line, sending a shockwave through the floor. For three days, he waited in the rubble, pressing his palms against cold steel beams until his skin registered that exact, unyielding chill. The experience left him with disconnected images: a collapsed stairwell, the acrid taste of burnt cotton on his tongue, and the deafening crack of buckling concrete. Rather than settling into a coherent timeline, the event lodged in his mind as shattered pieces that refused to align. Whenever the taste of ash surfaced, it did not arrive as a recollection but as an immediate, overwhelming presence, as if the fire were still burning around him. Because the memory felt so intensely present and fractured, Karim found himself caught in a relentless loop. The vivid, present-tense recall of the event triggered sudden waves of nausea and the return of intrusive memories whenever the thermostat dropped to that specific cold threshold. The intrusive nature of these sensations guaranteed that his threat system would ignite, forcing his eyes to dart toward windows and doorways as he constantly scanned for structural cracks or unfamiliar faces. This hypervigilant state made escape route planning feel non-negotiable; he had to map every exit before he could sit down. The relentless cognitive load and physical panic drove him to his only perceived relief, so he would retreat to his pattern table and work hard at keeping busy with late-night fittings just to outrun the panic. Now, at his midtown design studio, the cycle had become deeply entrenched. When the heating system released that specific chill or a delivery truck backfired outside, the intrusive memory would strike again, accompanied by the familiar sickening churn in his stomach. The sudden physical surge pushed him toward his rigid routines, leading him to throw himself into self-harm by digging scissors into his forearm just to release the overwhelming feelings, or to meticulously check the deadbolts and window latches over and over. Faced with this cognitive paralysis, his difficulty concentrating made client contracts blur, which in turn forced him to rely even more heavily on checking locks to create a false sense of order. His relentless busyness in the garment workshop temporarily dulled the taste of ash, but the suppression only guaranteed that the next memory would return even more violently. His constant scanning and escape-route planning made it impossible to process the past, which pulled the traumatic memory back into his awareness, while his avoidance habits cemented his perception that danger was always just beyond the threshold of his attention. Over the months, these habits quietly eroded his professional life, leaving his showroom empty and his phone unanswered. He finally walked into the clinic because his hands were shaking too badly to hold a tracing wheel, and the silence in his apartment had become unbearable. He was hoping to untangle the knot of memories that felt so real, afraid that if he stopped moving or checking, the past would swallow him whole, but he was desperate to reclaim the quiet space where he could finally sit still without bracing for collapse.
